purpose: Defines two small helpers: topScores returns the n largest numbers from a list using a hand-written sort, and hasDuplicates reports whether any value appears more than once.
summary: Both functions return correct answers for ordinary input, but each does more work than necessary. topScores sorts with bubble sort and also reorders the caller's array as a side effect, which is the most important problem here. hasDuplicates compares every pair of items, so doubling the input roughly quadruples the time. Both are quick fixes with built-in tools.

correctness.reason: topScores silently reorders the caller's array, and its inner loop bound is one too large. Results are right for numbers.

security.reason: Nothing here handles untrusted data, files, or the network.

performance.reason: Both helpers do quadratic work where n log n or linear time is possible.

readability.reason: Short, clearly named functions. Only var and the one-letter loop names get in the way.

issues.title: topScores reorders the caller's array
issues.explanation: `var sorted = scores;` copies the reference, not the array. Every swap in the loops below therefore changes the array the caller passed in.
issues.impact: Code that still needs the original order, such as a chart listing scores by date, now sees them sorted. The bug is silent and depends on who calls the function.

fix.description: Sort a copy so the input is never modified.

issues.title: Inner loop reads one element past the end
issues.explanation: The inner loop runs while `j < sorted.length - i`, so `sorted[j + 1]` is read at index `length` on the first pass, which is `undefined`. The standard bound is `sorted.length - i - 1`.
issues.impact: Comparing a number with `undefined` is always false, so numbers still sort correctly. If the comparison ever changes, or the list holds strings or objects, this off-by-one can produce wrong results or errors.

fix.before: for (var j = 0; j < sorted.length - i; j++) {
fix.after: for (let j = 0; j < sorted.length - i - 1; j++) {

issues.title: Bubble sort does quadratic work
issues.explanation: Two nested loops compare neighbouring items, so the work grows with the square of the list length. There is no early exit when a pass makes no swaps, so even an already sorted list takes the full amount of work.
issues.impact: For 10,000 scores that is around 50 million comparisons. The built-in sort needs roughly 130 thousand comparisons for the same list. A leaderboard that is re-sorted on every request will feel slow well before it looks large.

    for (var j = 0; j < sorted.length - i; j++) {

fix.description: Use the built-in sort on a copy. It also fixes the input-mutation problem. If you only ever need a small top n from a large list, a partial selection (a heap of size n) is faster still.

issues.title: Duplicate check compares every pair
issues.explanation: For each item the inner loop scans all later items. Without duplicates, that is about n × n / 2 comparisons.
issues.impact: A list of 100,000 items needs around 5 billion comparisons to prove there are no duplicates, which takes seconds. A set answers the same question in one pass.

    for (var j = i + 1; j < items.length; j++) {

fix.description: Compare the size of a Set with the length of the list. One behaviour differs: a Set treats NaN as equal to NaN, while === does not, so a list with two NaN values counts as having duplicates.

issues.title: Prefer let and const over var
issues.explanation: `var` is scoped to the whole function and is hoisted, so `i`, `j` and `tmp` are visible outside the loops where they are used.
issues.impact: Mostly a readability and future-bug risk. Reusing `i` or `j` by accident outside their loop would compile without any warning.

fix.description: Declare loop counters with let and values that never change with const.

issues.title: Inputs are not validated
issues.explanation: Nothing checks that `scores` is an array or that `n` is a sensible count. A negative `n` makes `slice(0, n)` drop items from the end instead of returning none.
issues.impact: Bad input produces a confusing result rather than an error, which makes problems harder to trace back to the caller.

fix.description: Reject unusable input at the top of the function.

positives.comment: The comment states what the function returns and in what order.
hasDuplicates stops at the first match instead of scanning the whole list.

complexity.explanation: Let n be the number of items passed in. In both functions an outer loop runs up to n times and an inner loop runs up to n times for each of those, which gives n × n steps. Neither function allocates anything that grows with n, so the extra memory is constant. topScores also calls slice, which copies at most the requested count, a cost that is small compared with the sort.

functions.name: topScores
functions.explanation: The loops always run to completion. There is no early exit, so even an already sorted list takes about n²/2 comparisons. It sorts the caller's array in place, so it adds no extra memory beyond the slice at the end.

functions.name: hasDuplicates
functions.explanation: If the first two items match, it returns immediately. When there are no duplicates, which is the common case, every pair is compared once, about n²/2 comparisons.

algorithms.name: Bubble sort
algorithms.evidence: Neighbouring items are compared and swapped inside two nested loops, so the largest remaining value moves to the front on every pass. Here the sort is descending.
algorithms.summary: Repeatedly walks through the list swapping out-of-order neighbours until the list is ordered.
algorithms.assessment: Simple and in place, but slow. It is only reasonable for a handful of items or teaching. This version also lacks the usual early-exit check that makes bubble sort fast on sorted input.

alternatives.name: Built-in sort (TimSort in modern engines)
alternatives.tradeoff: Much faster for large lists and thoroughly tested. Remember to pass a numeric comparator.

alternatives.name: Heap-based top-k selection
alternatives.tradeoff: Best when k is much smaller than n, because the full list is never sorted. More code to write.

alternatives.name: Quickselect then sort the top k
alternatives.tradeoff: Average-case linear. Worst case is quadratic unless the pivot is chosen carefully.

algorithms.name: Brute-force pairwise duplicate check
algorithms.evidence: Each item is compared with every later item using two nested loops, with an early return on the first equal pair.
algorithms.summary: Checks all pairs of items for equality.
algorithms.assessment: Correct and uses no extra memory, which is its one advantage. For anything beyond a few hundred items, hashing is a better fit.

alternatives.name: Hash set
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass and the fastest in practice, at the cost of memory proportional to the number of distinct items.

alternatives.name: Sort, then compare neighbours
alternatives.tradeoff: No hash table needed, but it reorders the data, so it needs a copy if the order matters.

limitations: This is a single snippet. Code that calls these functions was not visible, so the effect of the input being reordered on callers is assumed.
Complexity is worked out from the structure of the code. Real speed also depends on the runtime and the data.
